abstract.text: We analyze the effect of rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets, exploiting cross-market variation in import exposure stemming from initial differences in industry specialization and instrumenting for US imports using changes in Chinese imports by other high-income countries. Rising imports cause higher unemployment, lower labor force participation, and reduced wages in local labor markets that house importcompeting manufacturing industries. In our main specification, import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment. Transfer benefits payments for unemployment, disability, retirement, and healthcare also rise sharply in more trade-exposed labor markets.

thesis.text: Rising Chinese import competition from 1990 to 2007 adversely affected US local labor markets by reducing manufacturing employment and wages and increasing unemployment, nonparticipation, and transfer-benefit receipt.

citations.context: The past two decades have seen a fruitful debate on the impact of international trade on US labor markets (Feenstra 2010).
One factor limiting trade’s impact on US labor is that historically, imports from low-wage countries have been small (Krugman 2000).

Commuting zones (CZs), which encompass all metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas in the United States, are logical geographic units for defining local labor markets (Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013).
citations.reference_key: Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013

citations.context: Our identification strategy is related to that used by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), who consider the relationship between imports from China and innovation in Europe.

An alternative approach would be to use a Heckscher-Ohlin or a specific-factors model, as in Topalova (2005, 2010) or Kovak (2013), in which the mapping is strictly from trade prices to wages and employment.

In related work that uses data for 1990 and 2000, McLaren and Hakobyan (2010)fail to find significant effects of NAFTA on local US labor markets (though they do detect effects on industry wage growth).
As of 2010, 4.6 percent of adults age 25 to 64 receive SSDI benefits, and SSDI applications and awards are elastic to adverse labor market shocks (Autor and Duggan 2003 and 2010).

An alternative possibility, suggested by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), is that manufacturing plants react to import competition by accelerating technological and organizational innovations that increase productivity and may raise wages.

If trade with China increases the variety of inputs to which US producers have access, it may raise their productivity (e.g., Goldberg et al. 2010), increasing their demand for labor and partially offsetting the impact of import competition in final goods.

Using Gruber’s (2010) estimate that the marginal excess burden of taxation (required to fund transfers) is equal to approximately 40 cents on the dollar, the increase in transfers resulting from import exposure implies an increase in annual deadweight loss of $13 and $21 in these two periods, or $33 in total.
We estimate these voluntary responses by applying Hicksian labor force participation and hours elasticities of ηe ≈ 0.25 and ηh ≈ 0.50, respectively, drawn from Chetty (2012).

sections.summary: Introduces the China trade shock, summarizes the local-labor-market design, previews the main adverse employment, wage, participation, and transfer findings, and situates the paper in the trade-and-wages literature.
sections.title: Introduction and Contribution

source_span.end_text: In this section, we consider theoretically how growth in US imports from China affects the demand for goods produced by US regional economies.
source_span.start_text: I. Theoretical Motivation and Empirical Approach

sections.summary: Builds a monopolistic-competition trade model to derive product-demand shocks from China to US regional economies, highlighting imbalanced trade and the mapping from Chinese export supply to regional traded and non-traded employment.
sections.title: Theoretical Motivation and Empirical Approach

source_span.end_text: Following (2),our main measure of local labor market exposure to import competition is the change in Chinese import exposure per worker in a region, where imports are apportioned to the region according to its share of national industry employment:
source_span.start_text: B. Empirical Approach

sections.summary: Defines the import-exposure-per-worker measure, explains the 2SLS strategy using Chinese imports in other high-income countries, discusses threats to identification, and previews the gravity-based robustness approach.
sections.title: Measuring Import Exposure and Identification Strategy

source_span.end_text: II. Data Sources and Measurement
source_span.start_text: This section provides summary information on our data construction and measurement, with further details given in the online Data Appendix.

sections.summary: Describes UN Comtrade import data, the eight comparison high-income countries, commuting zones, County Business Patterns industry employment, Census/ACS labor outcomes, and transfer-payment data construction.
sections.title: Data Sources and Measurement

source_span.end_text: Table 2 presents initial estimates of the relationship between Chinese import exposure and US manufacturing employment.
source_span.start_text: III. The Impact of Trade Shocks on Manufacturing Employment

sections.summary: Presents 2SLS estimates showing that rising Chinese import exposure reduces manufacturing employment share; reports first-stage strength, falsification tests, controls for manufacturing share, demographics, routine occupations, and offshorability, and finds robust negative effects.
sections.title: Manufacturing Employment Effects: 2SLS Estimates and Robustness

source_span.end_text: The offshorability index used in column 5 measures the average degree to which the occupations in a commuting zone require neither proximity to a specific worksite nor face-to-face contact with US based workers.
source_span.start_text: population share in manufacturing falls by about 0.23 percentage points for each additional percentage point of initial employment in routine occupations.

sections.summary: Benchmarks the manufacturing-employment decline attributable to China, decomposes supply versus demand components, and compares China with other low-income, Mexico/CAFTA, and all other exporters.
sections.title: Benchmarking and Alternative Trade Sources

source_span.end_text: The results of Sections IIIA to IIIC suggest that the exposure of CZs to growing imports from China is a quantitatively important determinant of the decline in the share of manufacturing employment in the working-age population.
source_span.start_text: IV. Beyond Manufacturing: Trade Shocks and Local Labor Markets

sections.summary: Shows that trade-exposed CZs experience little population mobility but lower manufacturing and nonmanufacturing employment, higher unemployment and labor-force nonparticipation, and that effects are larger for noncollege adults.
sections.title: Local Labor Market Adjustment Beyond Manufacturing

source_span.end_text: One mechanism that potentially accommodates the rise in labor force nonparticipation following a rise in import exposure is enrollment in the Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI)program, which provides transfer benefits and Medicare coverage to working-age adults who are able to establish that their disabilities preclude gainful employment.
source_span.start_text: B. Wage Effects

sections.summary: Estimates wage effects, finding average weekly earnings decline with import exposure, manufacturing wages show no significant decline while nonmanufacturing wages fall, and discusses composition and local general-equilibrium mechanisms.
sections.title: Wage Effects

source_span.end_text: The decline in employment and wages in CZs facing growing import exposure is likely to generate an increase in residents’ demand for public transfer payments, a conjecture that is reinforced by the finding in Table 5 that CZs facing increased import exposure experience a rise in federal disability program (SSDI) recipients.
source_span.start_text: V. Public Transfer Payments and Household Incomes

sections.summary: Shows rising import exposure increases per-capita transfer receipts, especially SSDI, medical, retirement, and income assistance, while TAA is small; household earnings and wage/salary income fall and transfers offset only a small part.
sections.title: Public Transfers and Household Income

source_span.end_text: In this section, we consider alternative measures of trade exposure for US commuting zones in order to gauge the robustness of our results.
source_span.start_text: VI. Exports and the Factor Content of Trade

sections.summary: Tests alternate exposure measures including domestic plus international Chinese exposure, net imports, input-adjusted imports, gravity residuals, and factor content; results remain qualitatively similar, though coefficients vary.
sections.title: Alternative Measures of Trade Exposure

source_span.end_text: What do our results imply about US gains from trade with China?
source_span.start_text: VII. Losses in Efficiency from Use of Public Benefits and Involuntary Labor Force Nonparticipation

sections.summary: Quantifies deadweight losses from increased transfer take-up and involuntary nonparticipation, using tax-burden estimates, labor-supply elasticities, and conservative welfare-loss calculations.
sections.title: Deadweight Losses from Transfers and Nonparticipation

source_span.end_text: VIII. Conclusion
source_span.start_text: The value of annual US goods imports from China increased by a staggering 1,156 percent from 1991 to 2007, whereas US exports to China grew by much less.

sections.summary: Concludes that Chinese import competition had broad distributional and medium-run efficiency consequences for US local labor markets, beyond manufacturing employment alone, and may contribute to public anxiety about globalization.
sections.title: Conclusion

sections.title: Appendix Tables and Robustness

sections.title: Theory Appendix

abstract.text: We analyze the effect of rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets, exploiting cross-market variation in import exposure stemming from initial differences in industry specialization and instrumenting for US imports using changes in Chinese imports by other high-income countries. Rising imports cause higher unemployment, lower labor force participation, and reduced wages in local labor markets that house importcompeting manufacturing industries. In our main specification, import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment. Transfer benefits payments for unemployment, disability, retirement, and healthcare also rise sharply in more trade-exposed labor markets.

thesis.text: Rising Chinese import competition from 1990 to 2007 adversely affected US local labor markets by reducing manufacturing employment and wages and increasing unemployment, nonparticipation, and transfer-benefit receipt.

citations.context: The past two decades have seen a fruitful debate on the impact of international trade on US labor markets (Feenstra 2010).
One factor limiting trade’s impact on US labor is that historically, imports from low-wage countries have been small (Krugman 2000).

Commuting zones (CZs), which encompass all metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas in the United States, are logical geographic units for defining local labor markets (Tolbert and Sizer 1996; Autor and Dorn 2013).

citations.context: Our identification strategy is related to that used by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), who consider the relationship between imports from China and innovation in Europe.

An alternative approach would be to use a Heckscher-Ohlin or a specific-factors model, as in Topalova (2005, 2010) or Kovak (2013), in which the mapping is strictly from trade prices to wages and employment.

In related work that uses data for 1990 and 2000, McLaren and Hakobyan (2010)fail to find significant effects of NAFTA on local US labor markets (though they do detect effects on industry wage growth).
As of 2010, 4.6 percent of adults age 25 to 64 receive SSDI benefits, and SSDI applications and awards are elastic to adverse labor market shocks (Autor and Duggan 2003 and 2010).

An alternative possibility, suggested by Bloom, Draca, and Van Reenen (2011), is that manufacturing plants react to import competition by accelerating technological and organizational innovations that increase productivity and may raise wages.

If trade with China increases the variety of inputs to which US producers have access, it may raise their productivity (e.g., Goldberg et al. 2010), increasing their demand for labor and partially offsetting the impact of import competition in final goods.

Using Gruber’s (2010) estimate that the marginal excess burden of taxation (required to fund transfers) is equal to approximately 40 cents on the dollar, the increase in transfers resulting from import exposure implies an increase in annual deadweight loss of $13 and $21 in these two periods, or $33 in total.
We estimate these voluntary responses by applying Hicksian labor force participation and hours elasticities of ηe ≈ 0.25 and ηh ≈ 0.50, respectively, drawn from Chetty (2012).
